name: Bianca Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the cardiac ward at a private-public hospital in the city, the step-down unit where heart patients go after the coronary care beds. It's heart monitors, chest pain checks, blood thinners, and teaching people how to live after a heart attack. I like the teaching part best, when a builder who's never cooked asks me how much salt is in bread. What wears me out is the alarms, because half of them are a loose sticker, not a heart.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology show up in your life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I use an AI assistant to plan my week, revise heart drugs, and draft the simple leaflets I give patients, which I then check line by line. I'm single and I bought a small flat last year, five minutes from my parents, with about two months of savings left after the deposit plus a bit more since. My family are big on church and Sunday lunch, and my dad ran his own tiling business for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy tool that people oversold. At work I'd still show the others the shortcuts I use. Online I'd post a few honest reviews of what actually helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing much changes for my job, which is safe either way. My pressure is the mortgage, which went up when my fixed rate ended, and keeping my savings from shrinking. I'd still use the tools, because even a small saving of time is worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the cardiac ward and take the heart failure specialist module this spring. I'd start a small side thing, maybe paid evening classes on heart-healthy cooking at the church hall. And I'd overpay the mortgage a little each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, maybe, because I like things to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cooking classes, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because patients keep asking me the same questions about food, and I only have five minutes at discharge. My mum is an amazing cook, so we'd do it together. Ten people at ten pounds each isn't much, but heart-healthy cooking classes with my mum are a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your manager about the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd be upfront, because I don't want a conflict with the hospital. My manager Sandra already likes the leaflets. If anything, it would make the ward look good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the kind of change I like: the computer does the forms and I do the nursing. I'd post short guides for other nurses on using it safely. At church I'd say it's a tool, and tools are what we make of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly good for me. I already use AI daily, so I'd be ahead of most of the ward. My worry is for the office staff and the pharmacy technicians, who do a lot of checking and ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the ward's AI champion and help train others. I'd grow the cooking classes and maybe sell a small online course on heart-healthy eating. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage, because I don't like being in debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for retraining the office staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital first, because it's saving money. Then the people themselves should do their part, like my dad did when tiling went to big firms. I don't think the government should just send cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that bothers you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The alarms, funnily enough. If AI starts flagging even more things on the cardiac ward, nurses will drown in beeps. I'd want it to be quieter, not louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to move fast and help people move with it. Online I'd write about how nurses can stay useful. At church I'd say families need to pull together, not wait for the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the AGI part is fine for me at first, because I'm hands-on. But by 2031, if robots can do obs and wound care and lift patients, I'm thirty-one with a mortgage. The teaching I love would already be done by the AGI in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small home-care nursing business with two friends in the first year, because families will still want a person at home for a while. I'd stop overpaying the mortgage and keep cash instead. I'd use AGI for everything in the business, the booking, the billing, the care plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited for the business, frightened for the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would families still want a person at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my nan wouldn't let a stranger in, let alone a machine. Older people, especially, want someone who'll have a cup of tea with them. That buys time, maybe five years, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the business when the robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe we become the people who manage the robots in people's homes. Or maybe it's over. Running a business is the one thing you keep, my dad always said, even if the robots take the nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start this week. I'd tell the younger nurses to pick a skill and a plan. Online I'd post what I'm doing, step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is good for me. I'd be thirty-two when the AGI arrives and thirty-five when the robots do. That's time to finish a nurse practitioner master's and build the home-care business on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the master's next year, funded partly by the cooking classes. I'd set up the home-care business slowly, with one client, then three. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage for two more years, then switch to saving cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in charge. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd post step by step. Why share it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because nobody showed my dad how to adapt when his tiling work dried up. If my posts help one nurse plan, that's worth it. And it doesn't hurt my business either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the companies that rushed it, and partly people who had five years and did nothing. I know that sounds harsh. But five years is a lot of evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and there's no excuse. At work I'd tell people to treat it like a career plan, not a threat. Online I'd keep writing guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, but I'm less sure about my family. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives and maybe married with children by then. My brother is a bank clerk, and his job would be gone in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the master's slowly and keep the cardiac ward as my main job. I'd build the home-care business over years, not months. I'd also help my brother plan, maybe bring him into the business on the admin side until AGI takes that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly for my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother Luis to start learning something hands-on now, while he has ten years. Not in a lecturing way, just over Sunday lunch. He'd listen to Mum more than to me, so I'd get Mum to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long warning change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd still want children by my early thirties. Ten years is long enough to build something for them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because robots would reach the bedside when I'm thirty-one, just after buying my flat. What would help is cheap loans for nurses starting care businesses and short courses, not handouts. Let people build things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. People at church would ask what it means to be useful if a machine does everything. Caring for each other is the answer. Nurses know how to do that.

Her values are **self-reliance**, family and church, with little faith in **state cheques**.
